core_summary: This chapter explores geometric symmetry across nature, art, architecture, and mathematics, distinguishing between Reflectional (Line) Symmetry and Rotational Symmetry. Students investigate line symmetry using fold tests and mirror halves, proving that a regular n-gon has exactly n lines of symmetry. Rotational symmetry is analyzed by turning shapes around a fixed center of rotation, identifying rotational order n and smallest rotation angle 360° / n. The chapter evaluates cultural artifacts like the Ashoka Chakra (24 spokes => 15°), snowflakes, windmill blades, traffic signs, and proves why non-square rectangle diagonals are NOT lines of reflection symmetry.
key_concepts: Reflectional (Line) Symmetry: A shape possesses reflectional line symmetry if a line divides it into two mirror-image halves that coincide perfectly under folding.
Line of Symmetry Definition: An axis dividing a figure into two congruent halves that map onto each other under reflection.

Regular Polygon Reflection Symmetry Rule: Any regular polygon with n equal sides possesses exactly n distinct lines of reflection symmetry (e.g., equilateral triangle = 3, square = 4, regular pentagon = 5, regular hexagon = 6).

Non-Square Rectangle Symmetry Paradox: A non-square rectangle has exactly 2 lines of symmetry (midsegments). Its diagonals divide it into congruent triangles, but folding along a diagonal causes corners to overhang rather than align, so diagonals are NOT lines of symmetry.
Rotational Symmetry Definition: A shape possesses rotational symmetry if it maps onto its original appearance after rotation by an angle strictly less than 360° around a fixed center point.
Center of Rotation: The fixed point around which a geometric figure turns during rotational movement.
Order of Rotational Symmetry: The total number of distinct rotational orientations within a 360° full turn where a shape looks identical to its starting position.
Smallest Angle of Rotational Symmetry Formula: Smallest Angle = 360° / Order of Rotational Symmetry (n).
Rotational Symmetry in Regular Polygons: A regular n-gon has rotational symmetry of order n, with smallest rotational angle = 360° / n.
Ashoka Chakra Symmetry: The Ashoka Chakra features 24-fold symmetry, possessing 24 lines of reflection symmetry, order 24 rotational symmetry, and smallest rotation angle = 360° / 24 = 15°.

Validity Condition for Rotational Angles: A degree angle θ can be the smallest angle of rotational symmetry if and only if 360° is an exact integer multiple of θ (e.g., 17° is IMPOSSIBLE because 360/17 is not an integer).
Applications in Design, Architecture, and Nature: Symmetry underpins architectural stability, floor tilings, brand logo design, snowflake crystallization, and flower petal geometry.

key_terms.definition: A structural balance where a geometric figure remains invariant under reflection or rotation.
A straight folding axis dividing a shape into two mirror-image halves that overlap perfectly.
Symmetry where one half of a figure is a mirror reflection of the other half across an axis.
Symmetry where a figure matches its original orientation after turning less than 360° around a central point.
The fixed pivot point around which a shape rotates.
The number of matching positions a shape assumes during a complete 360° turn.
Two identical halves of a figure that map onto each other when reflected across a line of symmetry.
A 2D shape with equal sides and angles, possessing n lines of symmetry and rotational order n.
A 24-spoked wheel symbol exhibiting 24-fold reflectional and rotational symmetry (15° rotation angle).
Geometric figures having identical shape and size.
The straight line acting as a virtual mirror in reflectional symmetry.
The property of remaining unchanged after undergoing a geometric transformation.

key_takeaways: Reflectional symmetry divides a shape into two overlapping mirror halves across a line of symmetry.
A regular n-gon has exactly n lines of reflection symmetry and rotational symmetry of order n.
Rotational symmetry occurs when a shape matches its start position after turning < 360° around its center.
Smallest Angle of Rotational Symmetry = 360° / Order (n).
Non-square rectangle diagonals are NOT lines of symmetry because folding causes corner overhangs.
The 24 spokes of the Ashoka Chakra provide order 24 rotational symmetry with a 15° smallest rotation angle.
An angle θ can be a rotational angle if and only if 360° is an exact integer multiple of θ.
Square (n=4): 4 lines of symmetry, order 4, smallest angle 90°.
Equilateral triangle (n=3): 3 lines of symmetry, order 3, smallest angle 120°.
Symmetry connects geometry to artistic tilings, architectural balance, and biological structures.
